title: openEHR's anti-lock-in purpose puts the sovereignty thesis inside Better's core product
content:
openEHR exists to stop clinical data being locked into a vendor: the information model belongs to the standard rather than to the application, so the record can outlive whichever system currently writes to it. Better's core product is built on that standard.

The research's observation is about where the alignment sits. For most leads in the corpus, sovereignty is a stance about licensing or hosting; here it is the purpose of the product's central technology. The firm does not need to be persuaded that clinical data should not be captive, because that premise is why its product exists — which is why the workbook records the highest sovereignty score of any lead researched.

Commercially that makes the conversation additive rather than corrective. The open question is not whether the data should be portable but what happens to the decisions taken on it: openEHR makes the clinical record vendor-neutral without making the decision behind it attributable, and that is the gap a record layer fills. The lead is marked 'start here'.
